nameStory: Pink-sorrel gets its name from its lovely pink flowers and the distinctly sour taste of its leaves - 'sorrel' comes from an old French word meaning 'sour.' The tangy flavor comes from oxalic acid, the same compound that makes rhubarb tart and gives this plant's genus Oxalis its name (from the Greek word for 'sharp').
description: Pink-sorrel is a charming perennial with delicate pink flowers and shamrock-like leaves that fold up at night or when touched. This low-growing plant typically reaches 6-12 inches tall and spreads by underground bulbs to form small colonies. Originally from South America, it's occasionally found in New England gardens and has rarely escaped cultivation, making it quite uncommon in our region.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Soft pink flowers with five rounded petals that feel papery to the touch, blooming in loose clusters on slender stems that rise above the leaves

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three heart-shaped leaflets arranged like a shamrock that taste distinctly sour when chewed - they dramatically fold downward when touched or at dusk

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mats or small clumps that spread gradually, with leaves and flowers emerging directly from underground bulbs rather than obvious stems

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, pointed capsules that split open explosively when ripe, shooting tiny seeds several feet away with an audible pop

habitat: Extremely rare in New England, pink-sorrel is occasionally found in cultivated gardens, especially rock gardens or areas with well-drained soil. When it does escape cultivation, it prefers sunny to partially shaded spots with loose, moderately fertile soil.

seasonality.spring: New shamrock-like leaves emerge from underground bulbs, followed by the first flush of pink flowers in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with abundant pink flowers that open in morning sun but close on cloudy days or in late afternoon.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall, with seed capsules developing and explosively dispersing their contents.
seasonality.winter: Leaves die back completely, with the plant surviving underground as dormant bulbs until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Pink-sorrel's seed pods are natural catapults - when ripe, they explode with enough force to launch seeds up to 10 feet away, and you can actually hear them popping on quiet summer days!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded observation in New England, pink-sorrel is most likely to be confused with the much more common violet woodsorrel, but pink-sorrel's flowers are distinctly pink (not purple-violet) and the plant grows from bulbs rather than spreading by runners.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'wood sorrel,' pink-sorrel actually prefers open, sunny areas rather than woodland shade, unlike many of its cousins in the Oxalis family. The leaves are edible in small quantities but shouldn't be eaten regularly due to their oxalic acid content.
compareHints: Pink-sorrel stands out from New England's other woodsorrels primarily by its pink flowers - most relatives have yellow blooms, while violet woodsorrel has purple flowers. Unlike the creeping yellow woodsorrels that spread by runners, pink-sorrel grows from underground bulbs and tends to stay in tidy clumps rather than forming extensive mats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mountain woodsorrel differs from its yellow-flowered relatives in the genus by having white petals with pink veins instead of bright yellow ones.
Among New England's woodsorrels, upright yellow woodsorrel stands tall while creeping woodsorrel sprawls flat along the ground.
Slender yellow woodsorrel is smaller and more delicate than upright yellow woodsorrel, with thinner stems that tend to sprawl rather than stand erect.
Creeping woodsorrel differs from its upright cousin (Oxalis stricta) mainly in its prostrate, mat-forming growth habit versus the upright's tall, erect stems.
Violet wood-sorrel is easily distinguished from its New England relatives by its purple flowers - all other common wood-sorrels in the region have yellow flowers.
Unlike other woodsorrels in New England which have green leaves and yellow flowers, false shamrock stands out with its deep maroon foliage and white or pink blooms.
Among New England's woodsorrels, this is the only one with large pink flowers - all the others have either small yellow blooms or purple ones.
Great yellow woodsorrel differs from its more common relatives like upright yellow woodsorrel and slender yellow woodsorrel by its significantly larger leaflets and more spreading growth habit.
